To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cocaine-induced convulsant doses induce c-fos and c-jun mRNAs in limbic forebrain structures, and these mRNAs are followed by increases in preprodynorphin mRNA, but not preproenkepahlin mRNA, in many limbic forebrain regions.
c-fos, zif/268 and preprodynorphin/preproenkephalins are induced by convulsant doses of systemic cocaine.
c-fos, zif/268 and opioid peptide mRNAs were increased in limbic forebrain structures 3 h after a convulsant dose of cocaine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of action of cocaine, a drug of abuse that is highly addictive and is a leading cause of death and disease in the United States.
the role of immediate early genes and opioids in the development of cocaine-induced convulsant activity.
the role of opioid peptides in the pathophysiology of cocaine dependence, and with the use of these peptides as potential pharmacotherapies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the induction of c-fos and preprodynorphin mRNAs in limbic forebrain after cocaine-induced convulsive seizures is a function of the time elapsed after the last injection, and that zif/268 mRNA is not involved in this response.
convulsant doses of systemic cocaine induce c-fos and other immediate early genes in limbic structures and alter the expression of opioid peptides in limbic structures.
the convulsant effects of cocaine are associated with a widespread and complex pattern of immediate early gene and neuropeptide mRNA expression in rat brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immediate early gene and peptide responses to a convulsant dose of cocaine were temporally and regionally distinct.
the induction of c-fos and c-jun mRNA is an early event, occurring within the first hour after a convulsion.
convulsant doses of stimulant drugs alter the expression of immediate early genes, preprodynorphin, and preproenephalin mRNAs in limbic brain structures, and that these effects are time-dependent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
convulsant doses of drugs that are abused in humans can alter gene expression patterns that are similar to those seen in models of neurotoxicity and neurodegenerative disorders.
the limbic forebrain is highly sensitive to the convulsant effects of cocaine.
convulsant doses of a drug of abuse can alter the expression of immediate early genes and opioid peptides in limbic forebrain structures.
